passage: The car had not moved for twenty minutes on the flyover. Darshan kicked the seat. 'Papa, I'm bored!' Vishal looked in the mirror. 'Are you a bored-y boardy-snorey board?' Darshan stopped kicking. Vishal honked his own nose: 'Beep!' Darshan shrieked with laughter. 'Again!' Then he tried: 'Papa is a papaya-pie!' They both laughed so hard that the man in the next car smiled too.

qa.q: How long had the car been stuck on the flyover?
qa.a: It had not moved for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Darshan stop kicking the seat?
qa.a: He was caught by the silly sounding words and felt curious and amused instead of bored.

qa.q: What could Vishal try on the next long drive?
qa.a: He could play a rhyming game with silly words, letting Darshan make up his own, since nonsense sounds clearly delight him.

qa.q: How might the man in the next car see what was happening?
qa.a: He probably found their laughter cheerful and a nice break from the jam. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a young child enjoying silly word sounds and slapstick during a traffic jam.

passage: In their Delhi flat, Vinita Didi pulled Dhruv's socks over her ears and walked around saying, 'Where are my ears?' Dhruv rolled on the carpet giggling. She put a steel bowl on her head as a hat and pretended to sneeze, so it fell off with a clang. Dhruv laughed until he hiccupped. Then he put a sock on his nose. 'I'm an elephant!' he trumpeted.

qa.q: What did Vinita Didi pull over her ears?
qa.a: She pulled Dhruv's socks over her ears.

qa.q: What does Dhruv putting a sock on his nose show about how he felt?
qa.a: It shows he was delighted by the silliness and wanted to join in with his own funny idea.

qa.q: How could Vinita Didi keep this fun going safely?
qa.a: She could keep the jokes gentle and let Dhruv lead some silly ideas, taking turns being funny.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita Didi to play the clown for her brother?
qa.a: It seems fun for her too, and she likely enjoys hearing him laugh so hard.

grounding: Shows a young child appreciating physical comedy and absurd situations at home.

passage:
Monday: Sarita told Eshaan, 'Tidy your blocks and you get a star sticker.' He tidied fast and stuck the star on his shirt.
Thursday: she asked again, with no sticker. Eshaan kept building. 'What will I get?'
Next week, she said, 'Blocks away, or no park.' He scrambled to fill the box, glancing at the door. 'Now can we go?' he asked, holding out his empty hands.

qa.q: What did Eshaan get on Monday for tidying?
qa.a: He got a star sticker, which he stuck on his shirt.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan keep building on Thursday?
qa.a: There was no sticker, so he did not see a reason to tidy; he follows the rule mainly for a reward.

qa.q: What could Sarita do to help Eshaan understand why tidying matters?
qa.a: She could tidy with him and talk about how it helps everyone find toys, slowly adding reasons beyond stickers.

qa.q: What would change if Eshaan were a few years older?
qa.a: He might tidy because he understands it keeps the home nice for everyone, not only to get a sticker or avoid losing the park.

grounding: Illustrates a young child following rules mainly to earn rewards or avoid losing something, across days.

passage: The platform was packed, and the train was late. Ayesha gripped Mridul's hand. 'Hold on, or no chips.' He held tight, eyes on the chip packet in her bag. When a whistle blew and the crowd surged, she looked away for a second. Mridul let go to stare at a dog. Ayesha grabbed him back. 'Mridul!' He shrank. 'Are you going to scold me? I held most of the time!'

qa.q: What did Ayesha promise if Mridul held on?
qa.a: She said: hold on, or no chips.

qa.q: What was Mridul worried about when he shrank?
qa.a: He was worried about being scolded, which shows he follows the rule mainly to avoid trouble and get his treat.

qa.q: What could Ayesha say to help Mridul see why holding hands matters?
qa.a: She could explain calmly that crowds can separate them, so holding hands keeps him safe, not just earns chips.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel in that crowded moment?
qa.a: She probably felt a jolt of fear when he let go and relief when she grabbed him back.

grounding: Shows a young child obeying a rule for a reward or to avoid punishment, under crowded, time-pressed conditions.

passage: Under the mango tree near the village pond, Preeti had two ripe guavas from her Nani's tree. She had been saving them all afternoon. Yamini came and sat beside her, looking. Preeti held both guavas close to her chest and bit her lip. Then she sighed and held one out. 'You take this. It's the smaller one.' She paused. 'No, take the big one.' They ate side by side, slurping.

qa.q: Where did Preeti's guavas come from?
qa.a: They came from her Nani's tree.

qa.q: What does Preeti biting her lip and holding the guavas close suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she really wanted to keep both and felt torn about giving one away.

qa.q: How could Nani encourage Preeti's sharing without forcing it?
qa.a: She could notice it later and say it was kind, letting Preeti feel the good of sharing on her own.

qa.q: What might Yamini feel when Preeti hands her the big guava?
qa.a: She would likely feel surprised and happy, and closer to Preeti. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing a limited treat despite wanting it herself, in a village.

passage: In their Vancouver kitchen, only one cookie was left in the tin. Chen grabbed it first. His sister Leila's face fell. Chen looked at the cookie, then at her. He held it up and turned it round. 'I really wanted this,' he said slowly. Then he snapped it in half. One half was bigger. He held both out. 'You pick.' Leila took the smaller piece and smiled.

qa.q: How many cookies were left in the tin?
qa.a: Only one cookie was left.

qa.q: Why did Chen say 'I really wanted this' before breaking it?
qa.a: He was admitting his own wish for the cookie while deciding to share, which shows it was hard for him.

qa.q: Which part of Chen's choice was especially fair?
qa.a: Letting Leila pick her half gave her a real choice, which is a kind and fair way to split a treat.

qa.q: How might Leila see her brother after this?
qa.a: She may feel he cares about her, since he gave up something he wanted.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a limited treat even though he wanted it for himself, in Canada.

passage: On Wei's sixth birthday in Singapore, Aiko Ma had a plate of little cakes. 'You can eat one now, or wait until after dinner and have two.' Wei looked at the pink cake for a long time. He licked his lips. Then he pushed the plate away and went to play with his train, humming loudly. Twice he walked back and peeped. After dinner, Ma gave him two, and he beamed.

qa.q: What did Aiko Ma offer Wei if he waited until after dinner?
qa.a: She offered him two cakes.

qa.q: Why did Wei hum loudly while playing with his train?
qa.a: He was trying to distract himself from the tempting cake so he could wait for the bigger reward.

qa.q: What strategy helped Wei wait, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Pushing the plate away and playing elsewhere helped; next time he could ask for the plate to be put out of sight.

qa.q: How might Aiko Ma feel after keeping her promise?
qa.a: She may feel glad she kept her word, which helps Wei trust that waiting really pays off.

grounding: Illustrates a young child resisting an immediate temptation for a bigger delayed reward, in Singapore.

passage: In the school library corner, Chandrika Ma'am said, 'Anyone who wants can go to the sandpit now. Or stay for the whole story and get the first turn on the new swing.' Noor's friends ran out. Noor half stood up, looked at the door, then sat on her hands. She wriggled through the long story. When it ended, she ran first to the new swing and whooped as she flew.

qa.q: What reward did staying for the whole story bring?
qa.a: The first turn on the new swing.

qa.q: What does Noor sitting on her hands suggest about what she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a strong pull to run out with her friends and was holding herself back to wait for the swing.

qa.q: What could Chandrika Ma'am say to Noor afterwards?
qa.a: She could notice how hard waiting was and name how Noor managed it, so Noor remembers what worked.

qa.q: How might Noor's friends feel when they see her get the first swing?
qa.a: They might feel a bit jealous and wish they had stayed, or decide to wait next time.

grounding: Shows a young child resisting an impulse to secure a larger delayed reward, in a school setting.

passage:
First week: when Harsha Ma'am asked a question, Santosh jumped up and shouted the answer, pushing past others.
Two weeks later, he raised his hand but called out at the same time. 'Hand up, voice off,' she smiled.
A month on, Santosh sat on his mat, hand stretched high, lips pressed together, bouncing a little. When she called his name, he grinned and answered.

qa.q: What did Santosh do in the first week when a question was asked?
qa.a: He jumped up, shouted the answer and pushed past others.

qa.q: What does Santosh bouncing with his lips pressed together suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was eager to answer but working hard to control himself and wait his turn.

qa.q: What helped Santosh adopt the classroom habit?
qa.a: Harsha Ma'am's short, friendly reminder 'hand up, voice off' gave him a clear rule to practise over time.

qa.q: How might the other children feel about Santosh's change?
qa.a: They may find class calmer and fairer, since they also get a chance to answer.

grounding: Illustrates a young child moving from disruptive outbursts toward classroom etiquette over weeks.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the classroom, and their usual teacher was away. The new teacher had to shout. Tejas climbed under the table and refused to come out. 'I don't want to!' Hemant covered his ears but stayed on his bench, hand up, waiting. When his turn came, he shouted his answer over the rain. The teacher gave him a thumbs up and knelt to talk to Tejas.

qa.q: Why did the new teacher have to shout?
qa.a: Rain was hammering the tin roof, and it was very noisy.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling under the table?
qa.a: He may have felt overwhelmed by the noise and a new teacher, so he refused to cooperate.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Tejas join in?
qa.a: She could speak to him quietly, give him a simple job like handing out books, and invite him back without shaming him.

qa.q: How does Hemant's day differ from Tejas's?
qa.a: Hemant copes with the noise by staying seated and waiting his turn, while Tejas hides and refuses, so their mornings go very differently.

grounding: Shows the contrast between classroom etiquette and refusal to cooperate under noisy, unfamiliar conditions.

passage: When Abebe's grandmother visited their flat in Addis Ababa, he bowed and kissed her hand, the way his mother had shown him. 'Good afternoon, Ayat.' Their neighbour Fatima, a teacher, sat with them for coffee. When she spoke to him, he looked at her and listened till she finished. He wanted to tell about his toy truck, but he waited until the grown-ups paused, then said softly, 'Excuse me.'

qa.q: Who was Fatima?
qa.a: She was their neighbour, a teacher, who sat with them for coffee.

qa.q: What does Abebe waiting until the grown-ups paused suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to share his news but understood that elders should not be interrupted, so he held back.

qa.q: How could his family encourage his respectful manners?
qa.a: They could thank him and give him a real chance to talk after he says 'Excuse me', so politeness feels worthwhile.

qa.q: How might Ayat feel when Abebe greets her this way?
qa.a: She would likely feel honoured and warm towards her grandson.

grounding: Illustrates a young child showing polite deference to elders through greeting, listening and a soft tone, in Ethiopia.

passage: At the school gate, Hrithik folded his hands. 'Good morning, Yamini Ma'am!' She smiled. In class, when she read the rules for sports day, he sat still with his eyes on her. His friend whispered a joke; Hrithik shook his head and kept listening. Later, when Ma'am said his name wrong on the list, he said, 'Ma'am, it's Hrithik with an H,' in a small, polite voice.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say at the school gate?
qa.a: He folded his hands and said, 'Good morning, Yamini Ma'am!'

qa.q: Why did Hrithik shake his head at his friend's joke?
qa.a: He wanted to listen respectfully to his teacher rather than join in the whispering.

qa.q: What went well in how Hrithik corrected the teacher?
qa.a: He spoke up about his name but kept his voice small and polite, showing respect while still being heard.

qa.q: How might Yamini Ma'am see Hrithik?
qa.a: She probably sees him as a respectful, attentive child and appreciates the gentle correction. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child's polite deference to a teacher through greetings, attentive listening and respectful tone.

passage:
Teacher's note, Lavanya Ma'am, KG
Today after painting, Siddharth took the dirty water cups to the sink without being asked and wiped the table with a cloth. He put the class scissors back in their box, counting them. At lunch he picked up two wrappers from the floor, even though they weren't his, and put them in the bin. 👍 I've made him 'helper of the week'.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do with the class scissors?
qa.a: He put them back in their box, counting them.

qa.q: What does Siddharth picking up wrappers that weren't his suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he cares about keeping the shared space clean, not only about his own things.

qa.q: How could Lavanya Ma'am encourage other children too?
qa.a: She could rotate the 'helper' role so every child practises small jobs and feels trusted.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's parents respond to this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and might give him small jobs at home as well.

grounding: Illustrates a young child helping with chores, caring for shared classroom property and keeping surroundings clean.

passage: At dawn in their village, Kavitha swept the courtyard with a long broom. Keerthana, six, carried the small brass pot to fill the tulsi plant. She put her slippers neatly by the door. Before school she wiped her slate, which she shared with her cousin, and wrapped the chalk in a cloth. 'Amma, I put the broom back too,' she called. Kavitha smiled and handed her a piece of jaggery.

qa.q: What did Keerthana carry to the tulsi plant?
qa.a: She carried the small brass pot to fill it.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be feeling when she calls out about the broom?
qa.a: She probably feels proud of helping and wants Amma to notice.

qa.q: How could Kavitha keep Keerthana's help going as she grows?
qa.a: She could give her slightly bigger jobs over time and thank her, so helping becomes part of her day.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's cousin see her care with the shared slate?
qa.a: The cousin would likely appreciate finding the slate clean and the chalk safe.

grounding: Shows a young child doing small household chores and caring for shared property in a village home.

passage: "Ayesha, you think reading is hard? Let me tell you," said Irfan Nana, settling back. "When I was eight, I could not read at all. Letters looked like ants to me. My teacher, Master-ji, taught me after school under the lantern. 'Ka... ma... la.' I said each sound, then slowly joined them. 'Kamal!' I was so excited, I shouted it. Then words became lines. Then one day, I read a whole story about a clever crow, and I could tell my mother what happened in it. She cried."

qa.q: What story did young Irfan read all the way through?
qa.a: He read a whole story about a clever crow.

qa.q: Why did young Irfan shout 'Kamal!'?
qa.a: He felt thrilled because, for the first time, the sounds he joined made a real word he could read.

qa.q: What could Ayesha take from Nana's story if reading feels hard?
qa.a: She could practise sound by sound and join them slowly, since that is how Nana moved from letters to stories.

qa.q: Why might Nana's mother have cried?
qa.a: She may have felt deep joy and relief that her son, who could not read, could now understand and retell a whole story.

grounding: Illustrates a child moving from decoding letters into sounds to fluent reading and comprehension, told by a grandfather.

passage: The power went out during homework time. Pema, eight, held a torch over her storybook while her little sister Charu leaned in. 'Read it, Didi!' Pema traced the line with her finger. 'The... f-f-fox... wanted... the grapes.' A long word stopped her. 'Un-reach-able.' She said it twice, then read on smoothly. At the end Charu asked, 'Why did the fox say the grapes were sour?' Pema thought. 'Because he couldn't get them, so he pretended he didn't want them.'

qa.q: What did Pema use to see the page?
qa.a: She held a torch over her storybook.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the long word stopped her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She may have felt stuck for a moment but determined, since she broke it into parts and said it twice before reading on.

qa.q: What reading strategy helped Pema, and how could Charu use it later?
qa.a: Breaking a long word into chunks helped; Charu can try the same when she meets hard words.

qa.q: What would change if Pema could only read the words but not explain the story?
qa.a: She could not answer Charu's question, and the story would not mean much to either of them.

grounding: Shows a child decoding a hard word and then understanding the story, despite a power cut.

passage: Last year I thought maths was only counting on fingers. Then Amma made four parathas and there were six of us: me, Suraj, Amma, Appa, Paati and Thatha. Suraj said, 'Not enough!' I looked at the plate and thought, what if we cut each into halves? That made eight pieces. Six people, eight pieces. Two left over. I felt so clever. Appa asked, 'And what if Thatha wants two?' I counted again. Then only one left. Now when I see fractions in class, I think of parathas.

qa.q: How many parathas did Amma make?
qa.a: She made four parathas.

qa.q: Why did the narrator feel clever?
qa.a: They worked out by themselves that cutting each paratha into halves made eight pieces, enough for six people.

qa.q: How could a teacher use this kind of example in class?
qa.a: They could use everyday food sharing to teach fractions and division, so the ideas feel real.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when he saw the problem solved?
qa.a: He might feel relieved that everyone would eat, and perhaps a bit impressed by his sibling. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a child moving from counting to understanding division and fractions through sharing food.

passage:
Tuition note by Minakshi Ma'am, for Suraj's parents
Suraj used to add 7 plus 7 plus 7 plus 7 on his fingers and lose count. This week I laid out four rows of seven beads. He looked, then said, 'It's four sevens! Twenty-eight!' He tried 4 times 6 on his own with beads and then without. Then he did 3 times 5 in his head, frowning, and got it right. He also asked if subtraction can be done in groups. 👍 I have given him some practice sheets.

qa.q: How many rows of beads did Minakshi Ma'am lay out?
qa.a: She laid out four rows of seven beads.

qa.q: What does Suraj's question about subtraction in groups suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was curious and excited, and was starting to see numbers as groups rather than only counting.

qa.q: Why were beads a good choice for teaching multiplication?
qa.a: They let Suraj see repeated groups at once, which helps him move beyond counting one by one.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents feel after reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel encouraged by his progress and his curiosity.

grounding: Shows a child moving from counting to understanding multiplication as groups, in a tutor's note.

passage: When I was eight, Kashish Akka would tell me, 'Bring the bucket, fill it halfway, add the soap, then bring the mug.' I'd come back with just the bucket. She'd sigh. This year, in science, Ma'am gave us five steps to grow a bean. I whispered them to myself and counted on my fingers: soak, wrap, wet, dark, check. I didn't miss one, even when my partner kept chatting about cricket. My bean sprouted first, and I felt ten feet tall.

qa.q: How many steps did the teacher give for growing a bean?
qa.a: She gave five steps.

qa.q: Why did the narrator whisper the steps and count on their fingers?
qa.a: They wanted to hold all the steps in mind so they would not forget any, as they used to.

qa.q: What memory trick could the narrator teach a younger child?
qa.a: They could teach saying the steps quietly and counting them on fingers, since that helped them follow multi-step instructions.

qa.q: How might Kashish Akka see the narrator's change?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased and relieved that her younger sibling can now follow longer instructions.

grounding: Illustrates a child developing working memory to follow multi-step instructions over time.

passage:
Classroom note by Nirmala Ma'am, Class 3
In June, Urmila could only follow one step at a time and often drifted off during group work. Today I gave three steps: take out your ruler, draw a square, colour one half. She did all three while I watched, then checked her work against the board without being reminded. She stayed on her task for the full twenty minutes. When I said well done, she looked shyly pleased. 😊

qa.q: How many steps did Nirmala Ma'am give today?
qa.a: She gave three steps.

qa.q: What does Urmila looking shyly pleased suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud of her progress but a little embarrassed by the praise.

qa.q: How could Nirmala Ma'am keep building Urmila's attention?
qa.a: She could slowly add a fourth step and keep praising her effort, not just the result.

qa.q: How might Urmila's group-work partners notice the change?
qa.a: They may find her more helpful and focused, and enjoy working with her more.

grounding: Shows a child's growing attention span and ability to follow multi-step instructions, noted by a teacher.
